headline: KB Financial: nine-month profit up 10% to ₩5.6 trillion with fees up 38%, as buybacks keep shrinking the share count
takeaway: Third-quarter profit rose 4% to ₩1.76 trillion and nine-month profit 10% to ₩5.64 trillion. Diluted EPS grew faster, up 9% in the quarter to ₩4,851, because KB has been buying back and cancelling shares under Korea’s value-up programme. The ADRs rose 3.8%.
results: KB Financial Group reported profit attributable to shareholders of ₩1,758.9 billion for the third quarter, up 4.3% from ₩1,686.0 billion, and ₩5,643.5 billion for the first nine months, up 10.2%. Diluted earnings per share were ₩4,851 in the quarter against ₩4,458 a year earlier, and ₩15,439 for nine months against ₩13,403.

Net interest income rose 5.1% in the quarter to ₩3,507.1 billion. Net fee and commission income rose 14.2% to ₩1,126.6 billion, and over nine months fees grew 38% to ₩4,087.8 billion. Net insurance income rose 47% in the quarter to ₩474.9 billion. Nine-month provisions for credit losses fell to ₩1,576.3 billion from ₩1,675.2 billion.

Total comprehensive income attributable to shareholders fell to ₩772.0 billion in the quarter from ₩1,513.3 billion, reflecting valuation changes on securities. Over nine months KB bought back ₩1,044.9 billion of its own shares, cancelled ₩814.5 billion, and paid ₩967.3 billion of annual and quarterly dividends.
mgmt: KB’s quarterly filing consists of reviewed financial statements rather than a management commentary, so the strategic message comes from capital allocation. The group continued to return capital through quarterly dividends, the purchase of treasury shares and their cancellation, in line with the shareholder-return commitments Korean financial groups made under the government’s Corporate Value-up Programme.
The group also issued ₩404 billion of new hybrid capital and redeemed ₩693 billion of older hybrids during the nine months, managing its capital structure while returning cash.
view: Korean banks spent a decade trading at a fraction of book value — the so-called Korea discount — because they hoarded capital, paid low dividends and were seen as instruments of government policy. KB is the clearest example of how that is changing. Cancelling treasury shares, rather than holding them, is the important detail: it permanently reduces the share count, which is why EPS grew 9% in a quarter when profit grew 4%. Combined with quarterly dividends, KB is now returning a large share of earnings to shareholders.

The earnings mix is improving as well. Interest income growth of 5% is modest, reflecting regulatory pressure to limit household lending and the Bank of Korea’s rate cuts, but fees up 38% over nine months and insurance income rising show the benefits of KB’s diversified model across banking, securities, insurance and card businesses. Lower credit provisions suggest asset quality is holding up despite pressure in Korea’s real-estate project-finance market.

The risks are domestic. Korean household debt is among the highest in the world, the property market remains fragile, and regulators can push banks to support borrowers or lend to favoured sectors. The fall in comprehensive income also shows sensitivity to bond and equity valuations. Still, at single-digit earnings multiples and with capital returns rising, KB offers investors one of the more direct ways to benefit if the Korea discount continues to narrow.
watch: Watch the full-year shareholder-return announcement in February, net interest margin as the Bank of Korea’s rate path evolves, and credit costs in property project finance.
